title: Trump’s summer of tariffs means trade uncertainty is here to stay
gist: After the US Supreme Court struck down the 2025 'Liberation Day' emergency-powers tariffs, the Trump administration rebuilt an across-the-board tariff wall through a rotating stack of legal authorities — section 122, section 301 forced-labour and excess-capacity cases, section 338 of Smoot-Hawley, and national-security pharma tariffs — leaving an effective US tariff rate near 10.8 per cent and a 10-12 per cent floor on the 60 economies supplying 99 per cent of US imports. The core investable claim is not the level but the regime: the administration is deliberately imposing new tariffs faster than courts can strike down old ones, and Congress is ceding rather than reclaiming trade power, so policy unpredictability persists across future administrations.

themes.theme: Legal-authority rotation after the SCOTUS defeat

insights.claim: The US Supreme Court struck down Trump's use of an emergency powers act to impose the April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariffs by executive order, forcing the administration to rebuild the tariff wall on different statutory ground rather than abandoning it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Legal wins against tariffs reset the mechanism, not the tariff level — do not trade court rulings as a durable de-escalation signal.
insights.quote: The court struck down his use of an emergency powers act to declare wide-ranging tariffs via an executive order on ‘Liberation Day’ in April 2025.
insights.locator: From ‘Liberation Day’ to Section 301

insights.claim: Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 lets the US president impose up to 15 per cent tariffs on all imports for a maximum of 150 days to address 'fundamental international payments problems', and the administration used it from February 2026 as a stopgap global tariff that expired in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Section 122's hard 150-day clock creates predictable policy cliff dates — map the expiry calendar of each authority to anticipate the next tariff reshuffle.
insights.quote: Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 15 per cent on all imports for up to 150 days ‘to address fundamental international payments problems.’
insights.locator: July was a big month for US trade policy

insights.claim: The administration revived section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff act — a previously unused legal authority — to impose 50 per cent levies on various Canadian goods, showing that dormant statutes are now live tools.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Assume the legal-authority pipeline is deeper than markets price; screening exposure by statute already used will understate tail risk.
insights.quote: the administration cited a previously unused legal authority (section 338 of the notorious 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff act) to declare 50 per cent levies on various Canadian goods
insights.locator: Canada, Brazil, EU, China

insights.claim: The administration's implicit strategy is to keep tariff levels elevated by imposing new tariffs faster than courts can overturn the old ones, making litigation a speed bump rather than a constraint.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Price tariff risk as a persistent regime, not a series of resolvable legal events; hedges should be structural rather than tied to case outcomes.
insights.quote: it appears that the administration aims to maintain elevated tariff levels by imposing new tariffs faster than courts can overturn old ones
insights.locator: Exemptions and challenges

insights.claim: The first completed section 301 investigation accused 59 countries plus the European Union of permitting imports of goods allegedly produced with forced labour elsewhere — deliberately targeting countries rather than the firms actually using forced labour.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Because liability attaches to jurisdictions, not supply chains, corporate compliance and audited sourcing offer no tariff relief — country-of-origin exposure is the only variable that matters.
insights.quote: The investigation did not, crucially, focus on firms using forced labour. Instead, it accused 59 countries and the European Union of permitting the import of goods allegedly produced with forced labour elsewhere.
insights.locator: The first section 301 investigation to be completed

insights.claim: Tariffs implemented on 24 July 2026 reinstituted a 10-12 per cent minimum tariff on 60 economies that together supply 99 per cent of US imports, effectively recreating a universal tariff floor.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A ~10-12 per cent global import floor is now the baseline for US margin and CPI modelling regardless of sourcing shifts, since almost no trading partner is exempt.
insights.quote: they reinstituted a 10-12 per cent minimum tariff on the 60 economies, which together provide the US with 99 per cent of its imports
insights.locator: On 24 July, the administration implemented tariffs

insights.claim: Countries and the EU that actually enacted or strengthened forced-labour enforcement were still hit with the tariffs, demonstrating that policy compliance does not earn exemption.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite trade-policy relief on the assumption that a partner's regulatory concessions will de-escalate — the stated rationale is not the operative one.
insights.quote: This applied even to the countries (and the EU) that had moved to enact or beef up enforcement of forced labour bans.
insights.locator: This applied even to the countries

insights.claim: The overall US effective tariff rate is estimated at 10.8 per cent, but because forced-labour tariffs stack on top of previous measures, individual countries face materially higher rates.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Headline effective-rate figures understate dispersion; country-level stacked rates are the relevant input for single-name importer cost models.
insights.quote: while estimates put the overall US effective tariff rate at 10.8 per cent, some countries face much higher tariffs
insights.locator: Canada, Brazil, EU, China

themes.theme: Country and sector targeting: Canada, Brazil, EU, pharma

insights.claim: The 50 per cent Canadian tariffs were justified partly by Canadian public boycotts and Canada's retaliation over prior tariffs, meaning consumer sentiment and counter-measures in a partner country now themselves trigger further US tariffs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Retaliation is escalatory rather than deterrent in this regime — expect partner governments to face domestic pressure that mechanically worsens their tariff exposure.
insights.quote: some longstanding trade irritants, others related to Canadian public boycotts and retaliation over prior tariffs
insights.locator: Canada, Brazil, EU, China

insights.claim: The White House imposed a 25 per cent tariff on some Brazilian goods, widely read within Brazil as politically motivated ahead of the country's upcoming elections.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Brazilian asset risk now carries a US electoral-interference channel; watch the Brazil election calendar as a tariff catalyst, not just a domestic one.
insights.locator: The White House also put a 25 per cent tariff

insights.claim: Tariffs on pharmaceuticals from certain companies, justified under national security law, began taking effect on 31 July 2026 with some rates as high as 100 per cent, and a separate section 301 investigation targets German pharmaceuticals in response to German drug-cost containment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Pharma tariffs are company-specific and can reach 100 per cent — a stock-level, not sector-level, risk, with German drugmakers a named next target.
insights.quote: On 31 July, tariffs on pharmaceuticals from certain companies – justified under a different law focused on national security concerns – began to take effect. Some are as high as 100 per cent.
insights.locator: Pharmaceuticals have also been targeted

insights.claim: An unfinished 'excess capacity' section 301 investigation covers 16 economies including China, India, Japan and the EU and could produce high tariff outcomes, while a restarted 2019 'digital protectionism' case would chiefly target EU members and Canada.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Two named pipelines of pending tariff action give a watchlist of jurisdictions and sectors where risk is not yet in the price.
insights.quote: An ‘excess capacity’ section 301 investigation targeting 16 economies including China, India, Japan and the EU is still in process, with potentially high tariff outcomes.
insights.locator: More is on the way

insights.claim: Trump responded to the EU's July fines on Google by suggesting additional tariffs, tying EU digital enforcement against US tech firms directly to trade retaliation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: EU regulatory actions against US tech are now a transmission channel into EU-wide tariff risk — a cross-asset link between Big Tech antitrust headlines and European exporters.
insights.locator: President Trump’s response to EU fines on Google

themes.theme: US-China truce degrading at the edges

insights.claim: The US applied 12.5 per cent forced-labour tariffs to Chinese goods and banned Chinese-made humanoid robots, while China continued building out its capacity to restrict critical minerals flows.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Humanoid robotics is now an explicit trade-restricted category and critical-minerals leverage remains China's live counter-weapon — both are supply-chain chokepoints to monitor.
insights.quote: in addition to putting 12.5 per cent forced labour tariffs on Chinese goods, the US banned Chinese-made humanoid robots
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Washington and Beijing nibbled

insights.claim: Senior US-China meetings produced no progress on agricultural trade or Washington's planned Board of Trade to manage the relationship, with former US negotiator Ambassador Wendy Cutler quoted as saying mere preservation of the truce has become the objective.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Lower the base case for a US-China agricultural or institutional breakthrough; the realistic bull case is only that the truce does not break.
insights.quote: ‘just holding the truce together has become the main objective.’
insights.locator: For its part, the Chinese government

themes.theme: Exemptions as the real profit centre

insights.claim: The new tariffs cover only about half of all goods imported into the US because of significant exemptions, so the exemption process — not the headline rate — determines actual corporate cost exposure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Company-level tariff impact is dominated by exemption access; firms with Washington relationships can materially outperform peers with identical supply chains.
insights.quote: The new tariffs – like the ones they replaced – cover about half of all goods imported into the US, with significant exemptions.
insights.locator: Exemptions and challenges

insights.claim: A Commerce Department Office of Inspector General audit of the first Trump administration's 2018-19 tariff exclusion practices warned of the 'appearance of improper influence in decision-making for tariff exclusion requests', and a recent New York Times report raised similar questions about the latest forced-labour exemptions including commodities like diamonds.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Exemption allocation is a documented governance risk — a live headline and reversal risk for any company whose margin depends on a granted exclusion.
insights.quote: warned of the ‘appearance of improper influence in decision-making for tariff exclusion requests.’
insights.locator: An audit of the first Trump administration’s tariff exclusion practices

insights.claim: The exemption regime is a deliberate two-sided design: it dampens domestic inflationary pressure while making implementation complex and opaque, giving the president his across-the-board tariff wall while importers absorb the chaos.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect tariff pass-through to CPI to be muted relative to headline rates, with the cost surfacing instead as importer margin compression and planning friction.
insights.quote: President Trump gets a new version of the across-the-board tariff wall he desires, while importers get chaos.
insights.locator: Overall, President Trump gets a new version

themes.theme: Congress cedes trade power — the ratchet

insights.claim: Twenty-five US states are among those challenging the new tariffs in court, but experts disagree on which challenges might succeed, leaving legal relief highly uncertain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Litigation headlines will generate volatility without resolving direction — fade single-ruling reaction trades.
insights.locator: The new tariffs are already being challenged in court

insights.claim: Congress moved in contradictory directions in July: Senator Ron Wyden's comprehensive bill to return trade power to Congress has no clear path forward, while a bill granting the president more tariff authority — including 100 per cent tariffs on top importers of Russian oil — advanced through the Senate with strong bipartisan support and only ten Democrats opposing.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The only trade legislation with momentum expands executive power; a 100 per cent tariff threat against buyers of Russian crude is a real, bipartisan risk for India, China and other importers.
insights.quote: a bill giving the president even more tariff authority to target Russia, including to put 100 per cent tariffs on top importers of Russian oil, began to move through the Senate with strong bipartisan support
insights.locator: At the same time, a bill giving the president

insights.claim: The political economy of tariffs is asymmetric: the pain is diffuse while the benefits are highly specific and therefore easier to organize around, which explains why a US public majority dislikes tariffs yet no anti-tariff coalition forms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reusable model: do not expect unpopular-but-diffuse-cost policies to be reversed by polling — watch concentrated beneficiaries instead.
insights.quote: the pain they impose is diffuse, while the benefits are highly specific and thus easier to organize around
insights.locator: This reflects the politics of tariffs

insights.claim: A majority of Americans, including independents and non-MAGA Republicans, dislike tariffs and support free trade in the abstract, yet oppose specific trade liberalization deals once real and imagined costs are attached.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Anti-tariff polling is not a leading indicator of policy reversal; liberalization deals face the same public resistance as tariffs.
insights.quote: A majority of US public opinion supports free trade in the abstract but opposes specific trade liberalization deals with their real and imagined costs.
insights.locator: This reflects the politics of tariffs

insights.claim: The more aggressively this administration uses tariffs, the harder it becomes for successor administrations of any party to abandon them — an institutional ratchet reinforced by Congress's unwillingness to affirmatively set trade policy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Model elevated US tariffs as a multi-administration structural feature, not a Trump-term cyclical shock; re-shoring and supply-chain capex assumptions should extend past 2028.
insights.quote: the more aggressive this administration’s use of tariffs becomes, the more difficult subsequent administrations are likely to find it to move away from them
insights.locator: Congress also bestirred itself on trade

insights.claim: US industry is adapting by internalizing uncertainty and negotiating case-by-case exemptions rather than lobbying against the tariff system, which entrenches the regime by creating a constituency invested in its discretionary machinery.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Corporate adaptation is itself a lock-in mechanism — the longer the regime runs, the lower the probability of repeal, so treat tariff costs as permanent in DCF assumptions.
insights.quote: more corners of US industry are getting used to building in uncertainty and negotiating with the administration for exemptions from tariffs
insights.locator: Contradictory Congress

insights.claim: The closing analogy frames US trade policy like climate change — the risk is not a single shock but permanently elevated 'heat and unpredictability all year round.'
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The tradable variable is volatility and planning risk, not the tariff level — favour optionality and flexible supply chains over point forecasts of rates.
insights.quote: As with climate change, the risk for US trade policy is that the world is left with heat and unpredictability all year round.
insights.locator: This means it’s going to get harder
